We introduce a novel paradigm for the invariance property of a classic machine learning problem, thereby creating a challenging and relevant optimization problem. This problem has been split into two distinct blocks and we propose an innovative method that addresses this problem through a combination of block coordinate updating and rotational augmentation. This approach results in an efficient algorithm for solving a challenging non-convex optimization problem with a unique structure that facilitates efficient solution finding. We test and evaluate our method through extensive numerical experiments conducted on real and synthetic data sets. These experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method as compared to other optimization techniques.

Our investigation into manually annotated data highlights that existing datasets contain inconsistencies in labeled data, a problem that affects machine learning performance. To address this challenge, we propose integrating semantic labeling with paraphrase tasks. Our research demonstrates a notable decrease in performance on initial datasets and an increase in accuracy when using our proposed approach to validate annotated labels. To further explore this phenomenon, we created a synthetic dataset with intentionally inaccurate annotations. Our findings show that machine learning models struggle to achieve high accuracy on this dataset, indicating a strong correlation between difficult paraphrase tasks and inconsistent annotations. Furthermore, our results reveal that machine learning models are more effective at identifying problematic instances when presented with a more challenging paraphrase task, and that our proposed method is a cost-effective way to validate large annotated datasets.

Creating accurate 2D outdoor maps for robots to navigate using visual information from cameras is a significant challenge. Most modern mapping techniques rely on simultaneous localization and mapping SLAM to process real-time visual data, but they have limitations, particularly in understanding the bigger picture and managing local vs. global navigation. To address this issue, a novel representation called HiTMap separates navigation into two levels, using a tree-like structure to manage mapping at different scales. In the HiTMap system, a parent node represents a coarsely mapped parent scene, while the child nodes depict the detailed maps of sub-scenes that make up the parent scene. Each node has its own motion estimator to handle navigation within its designated scene, eliminating the need to synchronize and synchronize the speeds of different nodes, which can vary. Furthermore, HiTMap can handle large-scale mapping by repeating the structure of the tree, rather than relying on a single, global map. We present a novel algorithm for optimizing the speed of each node in the HiTMap system, along with a proposed architecture for implementing the HiTMap system using deep learning techniques, and discuss potential optimization strategies.

We investigate the sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system to a local magnetic field near its node, utilizing the Ramsey effect. By analyzing the systematic error associated with a non-zero magnetic field, we examined various parameters including their impact on the fringe visibility loss. Our main finding reveals that an extremely small magnetic field, as tiny as $10^{-16}$ Tesla, can be detected with high precision near the node of a Mach-Zehender atomic interferometry pattern. This achievement holds true when the initial atomic state is a coherent superposition of two hyperfine levels within the ground state of Rubidium-87, and it holds under conditions relevant to state-of-the-art atomic interferometry experiments that achieve precisions on par with $10^{-17}$ in magnitude.

We analyze a Bayesian nonparametric method for inferring the components of a mixture density using a Dirichlet process prior. By examining the posterior distribution's properties, we show that this method inherently places a Dirichlet prior on the weights, which can lead to weight identifiability issues in certain cases. To address this challenge, we develop a novel algorithm that recovers the weights by employing a Markov chain Monte Carlo method to sample from the posterior distribution, coupled with an additional step of sorting the sampled weights. We then apply this approach to a weighted mixture model and establish the conditions under which the algorithm yields a unique ordering of the weights. Moreover, we investigate the theoretical properties of the algorithm by examining its convergence rate and establishing the consistency of the sorted weights.

The rapid evolution of GPU architectures has resulted in multiple levels of memory, varying in speed and capacity, yet programming models continue to treat all memory as uniform. This aging model fails to adapt to the changing memory landscape, causing performance, memory usage issues and limitations, especially when processing large datasets. In response to these challenges, a new dynamic allocation algorithm for shared memory called DynaSOAr has been developed. Compared to conventional GPU memory allocators, DynaSOAr exhibits a significant boost in performance and a notable reduction in memory usage. The algorithm's innovative feature allows for the automatic refactoring of existing code to take advantage of DynaSOAr's capabilities, thereby simplifying integration. The development of DynaSOAr is demonstrated through a case study where it was applied to the OpenSource CuDNN library. The resulting optimized version of CuDNN displayed a marked improvement in performance and memory efficiency, outperforming the original CuDNN by nearly 5 times in certain workloads while achieving comparable results in others.

Recently, research involving YSR states has focused on pairs of magnetic adatoms on the Cu(111) surface. To better understand these findings, we examined pairs of magnetic adatoms, specifically the configuration of two magnetic adatoms at opposite corners of a square, on a superconducting Cu(111) surface using a combination of ab initio calculations and tight-binding models. By examining the spatial distribution of YSR states and their corresponding spectra, we discovered that the presence of spin-orbit coupling results in the shifting of YSR state peaks in response to the orientation of the adatoms' magnetic moments. When the adatoms are positioned at opposite corners of a square, we found that the YSR state spectrum exhibits a particular pattern characterized by the interchange of peak heights for certain energy levels due to the interplay between the exchange and anisotropic energies of the adatoms. Additionally, we found that the shift in energy levels is directly proportional to the anisotropic energy of the adatoms, providing a means of extracting this information from experimental YSR state spectra following a theoretical analysis of model Hamiltonians.

Two planets, Kepler-37d and Kepler-37b, are characterized as the smallest double planet system known so far, with a record for the smallest habitable zone transiting mini-Neptunes. Located in a distant solar system, Kepler-37 is an older, low-mass, G-type star hosting the two planets, Kepler-37d, a rocky world with a size similar to that of Earth, orbits the innermost region of a stellar system, while Kepler-37b, a mini-Neptune with a size between Earth and Venus, orbits the outer region. Both planets were discovered through the Kepler Space Telescope's observations of a slight decrease in the star's brightness as planets passed in front of it. Kepler-37 is notable for being the oldest star hosting a habitable zone planet. Based on measurements of the star's rotation, Kepler-37 is estimated to be around 11.5 billion years old, indicating that the two planets formed in a different stage of the stellar system's evolution. Kepler-37's small habitable zone suggests that most mini-Neptunes located in similar stellar systems might have already been ruled out as potential candidates due to their larger sizes.

We used computational methods to simulate substitutional and interstitial carbon and nitrogen atoms in titanium dioxide in both its rutile and anatase forms. By comparing our results, we found that when these atoms occupy interstitial sites, they exhibit different reactivity than when they substitute for oxygen atoms. Specifically, we found that nitrogen atoms bonded to each other repelled one another and that a dimer formation was highly unlikely, which contrasts with anatase's ability to form dimers when carbon atoms are present. Our study suggests that interstitial atoms' location could influence the reactivity of titania, which may impact its reactivity with $N_2$ and $C$ but not with $CO_2$.

An analysis at the LHC of the semi-elastic process $pp\rightarrow j_1 j_2 \eta\rightarrow j_1 j_2 \mu^+\mu^-$ is presented, relying on 20.3 pb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS experiment at 8 TeV. After applying selection requirements, the background is estimated to be 1200 pm 400 events. Assuming all background is from the SM, the expectation is 1200 events with a pseudo-mean transverse momentum of 36.9 GeV, leading to a cross-section limit of 1.5 x 10$^{-4}$ pb for the flavor changing neutral current (FCNC) decay $t\rightarrow c\eta$ after imposing $\beta\gamma\geq 1.5$ on the neutral particle's decay products. For $\eta\rightarrow\mu^+\mu^-$ decays with a mass range 2.0-4.0 GeV, the branching ratio limit is 1.6 x 10$^{-4}$. Similar limits are derived for the $t\rightarrow u\eta$ decay channel.

In 2006, Kierstead and Shaffer proposed an open problem concerning the coloring of a graph with the fewest colors, given a subgraph of a certain type. Another constraint specified that the graph be triangle-free with a specific condition. We offer a preliminary step in addressing this issue by deriving a particular lower bound for a triangle in a graph while utilizing a limited color palette. Our approach involves using a combination of list-coloring and the "pigeonhole principle" to achieve this goal. As an additional contribution, we establish a lower bound for a graph that contains an odd cycle of $2k+1$ sides, where $k$ is a number greater than 1, but no such bound exists for cycles of 3, 5, 9, or any other odd number when $k$ takes on those specific values.

We investigated the limitations of accurately measuring mass in two types of quantum systems: qubits and qutrits. Utilizing the theory of general relativistic quantum equivalence principle, we examined the impact of errors on mass measurements for both qubits and qutrits. Our research discovered that qutrits can withstand noisier conditions while determining mass. Specifically, we found that qutrits could tolerate up to 10% error rates during measurements, in contrast to qubits which could only handle up to 5% error rates. Furthermore, our study revealed that the precision of mass measurements varies significantly with the energy levels' splitting, and that the most accurate measurements are achieved when the energy levels' splitting roughly matches the frequency of fluctuations caused by the quantum equivalent principle's curvature, which in turn depends on the quantum system's properties.

The polarization of positrons was measured following the interaction of circularly polarized photons with electrons in a beam, using the Recollision Resonance (3R) scheme. A maximum polarization of 34.4% was achieved among the positrons, which could be beneficial for enhancing the stability of plasma based devices and allowing for the performance of certain experiments that utilize positron optics. Building on the initial findings, we have successfully intensified the polarization of positrons to over 40% and have identified methods to boost production to desired levels for specific applications.

We investigate the complexity of the group finitely generated by defining a polynomial function that estimates the number of steps required to reach a state of low complexity, despite working within the framework of polynomial diameter generation. This investigation yields two significant outcomes. Firstly, it has been proved that groups possessing polynomial diameter $d(n)$, where the variable holds a specific relationship with other important properties of the group's structure, specifically its class length, nilpotent subgroup size, and the length of cyclic subgroups, can be generated in a number of steps determined by a polynomial function of $n$. Secondly, it has been established that this property holds true for a broad category of groups characterized by their high level of stability, which includes nilpotent groups, groups possessing a finite number of conjugacy classes, and torsion groups.

A novel, ultra-low-voltage temperature sensor has been created using a single 32nm FinFET technology. This sensor can operate at as little as 0.4V and provides an exceptionally precise 0.14°C standard deviation across a broad temperature range, from 0 to 70°C. Its outstanding accuracy, with a mean inaccuracy of just 1.5°C over this temperature range, makes it an extremely efficient solution for a wide range of applications. This sensor features a distinctive, all-digitally-controlled bandgap architecture that uses a precise 16-bit digital thermometer to determine temperature readings. This design includes a handful of key innovations, such as a precise double-sampling current mirror, a low-noise voltage generator, and a highly accurate digital thermometer, to achieve the mentioned performance metrics. This temperature sensor can convert an analog temperature reading into a precise digital value, represented by 16 bits, and it has the added benefit of being completely immune to calibration procedures. With a maximum conversion time of just 12.8ms, this sensor can be used in a wide range of applications, including those requiring very low power consumption, such as wearable devices, as well as those needing high precision, such as medical equipment.

This research paper establishes a connection between topological groupoid extensions and certain types of geometric constructs known as gerbes, particularly those defined over topological stacks in the context of homotopy theory. Building upon the foundation laid by Moerdijk and Mrasek, we develop topological gerbes as refined constructs that incorporate additional information, effectively treating these constructs as equivalent classes of sheafified data. Consequently, this leads to the identification of a natural, one-to-one correspondence between the categories of topological gerbes defined over a given topological stack and the superordinate category of topological groupoid extensions. Notably, this relationship extends beyond basic gerbes to more intricate constructs, thereby broadening the scope of this connection.

To understand the relationship between molecular cores that give birth to massive stars and the formation of those stars, researchers need detailed information about the mass growth of these cores over time. A statistical study of 115 molecular cores that contain massive stars and surrounding younger or intermediate-mass stars was conducted using archival data from radio telescopes. By tracking changes in the mass of these cores and the surrounding stars, scientists discovered that cores with many surrounding stars grow more rapidly and are more likely to produce intermediate-mass stars. A model that takes into account the mass of the core, surrounding stars, and the movement of gas in the surrounding area was used to remove uncertain mass estimates and provide a more accurate view of core mass growth. Based on this model, scientists found that cores with many surrounding stars grow more rapidly and are more likely to produce intermediate-mass stars, and a threshold at which cores suddenly begin producing stars with 8 solar masses was discovered, indicating that stars with that mass may form suddenly rather than gradually.

This research paper examines the impact of applying basic differentiation and integration rules to zonal functions, a type of mathematical function that can be identified using the properties of orthogonal polynomials. Authors explore how these operations preserve the positive definiteness of zonal functions. Additionally, the paper provides a detailed investigation into the connection between zonal functions and classical polynomials, specifically focusing on Legendre and Gegenbauer polynomials. Further analysis is provided to illustrate the application of these findings to a specific problem involving the determination of minimum and maximum values of certain functionals.

The relationship between a liquid foam's structure and its ability to flow has been studied by analyzing the effects of surface tension and the size of bubbles on the flow's behavior. When the surface tension is high or the bubble size is small, the foam's ability to change shape quickly slows down. To better understand this connection, researchers defined a new metric called the "roughness factor" to help explain how irregularities in the surface of the foam's bubbles influence its flow behavior. By using high-speed cameras and sensors to track the movement of the foam, scientists were able to create a new method for estimating the roughness factor. This was achieved by studying the sound produced during the foam's deformation and comparing it to computer simulations of the foam's behavior. By applying this new approach, a more complete understanding of the interplay between the size of bubbles, the surface tension, and the flow's behavior became available.

Deep learning models, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks, have excelled in image classification tasks.  However, a significant drawback of these models is their lack of diversity, as they typically exhibit similar performance when employed individually.  Ensemble methods aim to overcome this limitation by combining multiple models to achieve enhanced performance.  This paper investigates the effectiveness of ensemble classifiers in enhancing the performance of state-of-the-art models for a specific image classification task.  By leveraging a diverse range of models, including ResNet, VGG, and MobileNet, and employing a novel ensemble approach that considers their distinct characteristics, our study achieves a notable improvement in performance.  Specifically, our ensemble classifier surpassed the individual models by 6.4%, and our proposed method also provided a clear rationale for selecting optimal ensemble components.  The code for this study is publicly accessible on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/ali Hosseini Ensembles-for-IR-Codes.

A rotating Hele-Shaw cell with a membraneized gap is studied as it experiences stress and instability, influenced by varying membrane tension. The model includes a range of rotating speeds and allows for different stable states, including steady circulation, chaotic behavior, and stationary patterns. Variations in membrane tension can cause these states to shift and even become unstable in themselves. The factors that determine the membrane's influence on the system's behavior include its tension, the viscosity of the fluid, and the rate at which it's stirred. The model reveals that even minor changes in membrane tension can significantly impact the system's behavior, leading to sudden and unexpected changes in its stability. The results obtained agree with previous experimental findings and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions at play in the Hele-Shaw cell. The tension's impact is particularly pronounced when the system is in a state of extreme sensitivity, exhibiting sharp transitions in response to minor changes in tension. The need for considering the membrane's properties as part of the system's dynamics is emphasized, in addition to the usual influences of fluid properties, in experiments and other studies involving the Hele-Shaw cell.

Cyclopentadiene's CCH to CN abundance ratio exceeds that of benzene by a factor of 40, indicating a greater presence of unsaturated bonds and a lower amount of CN derivatives. This difference is observed in both the interstellar and the local ISM, and can be attributed to the slower radiative destruction of CCH in cyclopentadiene, resulting from the longer lifetime of its excited state. As a result, the CCH to CN ratio in the interstellar medium may be an indicator of cyclopentadiene's abundance.

To enhance the performance of neural machine translation, particularly for lengthy sentences, a novel attention mechanism called look-ahead attention is presented. This approach directs the attention process towards unseen parts of the target sentence by incorporating forward information. To mitigate the risk of over-reliance on future elements, a causal constraint is imposed, ensuring that each attention matrix only considers portions of the target sentence that come after the currently processed part, but does not consider any that come before them. As a result, the innovation is dubbed a causal look-ahead attention mechanism. Experimental evaluations using the IWSLT 2017 English-to-German dataset demonstrate improved performance when applying causal look-ahead attention compared to standard attention, with notable gains when translating longer sentences. Additionally, the analysis shows that the benefit extends to sentences of varying lengths and cannot be attributed to other confounding factors such as increased depth. In fact, introducing the causal look-ahead attention mechanism is found to decrease the required network depth.

The success of grid computing relies on closely intertwining computational and networking research. A translational approach is crucial in developing and applying grid technologies, as it facilitates the feedback loop between theoretical research and practical implementation. This issue introduction outlines some of the key challenges facing grid computing, including security and trust issues, as well as opportunities and challenges presented by new applications and technologies. It also highlights some of the key research being conducted by the contributors to this special issue, such as the development of a grid virtual laboratory and the use of grid technologies for solving optimization problems.

The present study investigates the impact of the $f(R)$ gravity model's structure on the evolution of the universe by using a numerical method to solve the field equations. We explore three $f(R)$ models with negative and positive deceleration parameters and examine the behavior of the model by creating a graph showing the variation of the universe's density with the expansion scale factor. We observe that the $f(R)$ model results in a big rip if the model's viscosity coefficient exceeds a certain value. Our research reveals that the $f(R)$ model with a constant curvature term leads to a big bang model similar to the $\Lambda$CDM model but with a different initial condition. We also find that the $f(R)$ model with a power-law function of the Riemann tensor results in a big rip, causes the model to freeze, or leads to a combination of both behaviors, depending on the values of the model's parameters. We note that the $f(R)$ model with a negative deceleration parameter causes the model to freeze eventually. We create a graph showing the variation of the model's viscosity coefficient with the Riemann tensor and find that the model's viscosity coefficient changes sign when the Riemann tensor exceeds a certain value, indicating a sudden change in the model's behavior, which we attribute to a big rip phenomenon occurring at that point.

Using machine learning, we re-analyzed all quark models lacking a visible decay products final states to set a new lower limit on the cross section for dark matter nucleon scattering at $4.6\times 10^{-46} \,ext{fb}^{-1}$, a previous record held for certain $J/	au$ decay processes.

Multi-dimensional Fourier Shape Analysis (MFSSA) is an extension of the established method of Fourier Shape Analysis (FSA) for handling multiple dimensions. FSA has demonstrated its effectiveness across various applications, including the analysis of image features through Gaussian kernels. Following the same paradigm, MFSSA utilizes Gaussian kernels to map objects defined by multiple dimensions onto a circular domain, facilitating the application of Fourier methods. As a result, MFSSA can analyze complex data, such as remote sensing images and time series, by treating them as multi-dimensional vectors. Despite the advantages of this approach, implementing the original FSA algorithm remains computationally expensive due to its linear transform nature. In contrast, the modified version of FSSA, which has been optimized for faster execution, can now be employed widely in real-world contexts. The updated algorithm maintains its performance standards while exhibiting approximately 5 orders of magnitude improvement in computation efficiency. To showcase its capabilities, we have applied the optimized MFSSA to analyze real-world data, including a theoretical temperature curve and the Landsat7 image of the North Ireland map.

This research investigates the long-term direction of a specific type of random walk, which has independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) zero-mean increments, based on the walk's initial position. We examine the asymptotic behavior of the random walk in relation to its starting point and establish an analogue to the concept of the walk's being recurrent or transient. Our study establishes that the random walk's asymptotic direction becomes increasingly steady and unbiased as time progresses, provided a particular condition is met. This condition is shown to be necessary and sufficient to ensure the walk's asymptotic direction remains directed at a specific angle greater than zero, on average, and can be oriented with any desired angle in the range (0, π/2) through the manipulation of the walk's initial conditions.

To enhance the plasma efficiency of a plasma source, it's crucial to optimize the plasma parameters, specifically electron temperature and density. This study uses the Discrete Ordinate Formulation of the Boltzmann Equation to analyze a complex plasma device, specifically a helical mirror plasma source. By applying the method, we achieved a precise match between simulated and measured plasma parameters, indicating the approach's effectiveness for this specific source type. Nevertheless, the accuracy of this method may be questioned for other types of plasma sources. Nonetheless, this study demonstrates the utility of this method for optimizing plasma parameters for the helical mirror plasma source, and it is anticipated that a similar application could also benefit other plasma sources with a similar device configuration.

This paper presents a novel W-shaped network for detecting cell nuclei in cytological images, a task that is crucial for diagnosing diseases. The proposed model consolidates the advantages of both lightweight detection approaches and comprehensive feature extraction methods by introducing a unique structure with the initials 'W', which comprises three distinct modules to achieve high accuracy and efficiency. The initial lightweight network provides a coarse, preliminary detection, while the middle layer with a large receptive field helps identify key details, and the final module employs a feature extraction technique to achieve precise detection. The proposed model exhibits superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, demonstrating a significant boost in detection accuracy while concurrently reducing computational costs.

We investigate the dimension of the space considered in local gamma factors for specific irreducible representations of odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups. Our analysis reveals that the rank of these dimensions remains consistent when the context is extended to twisted forms. As a result, we find that the rank of twisted forms for local gamma factors equals the rank of non-twisted forms, which enables us to establish an isomorphism between certain representations. Our study also yields an improved comprehension of the space underlying local gamma factors, enabling us to create an equivalence between certain representations that was previously unestablished. Additionally, we establish relationships between spaces related to local gamma factors and the theta correspondence. Our research expands upon prior findings by Archin, Goldberg, and Gross, and the associated results and implications.

Deep Neural Networks have successfully addressed various tasks by leveraging subtle patterns in data, yet these insights remain difficult to interpret due to the complex, convoluted structure of learned representations. In contrast, traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks, which lack multiple layers of non-linear transformations, offer more accessible insights into the data. We propose a novel approach to reinterpret learned features from these models as being derived from graph convolutional networks, with the underlying graph determined by the network's architecture. By reinterpreting the learned features in this new framework, we can better understand the relationships among the variables represented in the input. To demonstrate the practical value of this approach, we apply our method to analyze a CNN used for a spatial analysis task and a fully connected Neural Network used for a genetic analysis task.

In gravity theory with a Chern-Simons term, we investigate how the behavior of rotating hairy black holes is connected to the entropy of the theory. Our findings indicate that these black holes' entropies are directly related to the entropy of pure Chern-Simons gravity, with the difference being specific to the specific dimension and a multiple of the angular momentum parameter. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the heat capacities of these hairy black holes and the heat capacity of pure Chern-Simons gravity. Our research approaches these discoveries through a novel, Einstein- Chern-Simons equivalence transformation that allows us to generate solutions for rotating hairy black holes from their non-rotating counterparts. This method also enables us to establish the exact entropy of these rotating hairy black holes, confirming previous findings based on a distinct, more restrictive assumption.

Ultrasound elastography aims to create detailed images of tissue stiffness by differentiating axial and lateral tissue displacements during compressions/releases. Initially, elastography methods were thought to accurately determine axial displacements and less precise lateral displacements. However, research demonstrating similar or even greater precision in estimating lateral displacements challenges this long-held assumption. This study introduces a novel statistical model using Gaussian processes in combination with circulant convolution operators to match the performance of axial and lateral displacement estimation. The proposed method's performance was evaluated under varying precision ratios between axial and lateral displacement estimations, and it outperformed the traditional method. The study also investigates the impact of training data quantity on model performance and successfully applies the novel model to demonstrate improved results in phantom elastography.

This paper introduces two novel specifications for verifying the correctness and security of programs against attacks, building on the concept of logical pseudocodes initially proposed by Dwork and his colleagues. We present two specific instances of these specifications, tailored for programs utilizing arithmetic operations, which provide insights into how differing logical pseudocodes can lead to incorrect or unsafe conclusions. To facilitate verification, we outline an approach that leverages these specifications in conjunction with mathematical proofs, incorporating techniques from the verification of computational protocols. Furthermore, we establish relationships between these specifications and previously proposed methodologies for verifying program correctness.

We introduce a pioneering one-pass algorithm that quickly builds a highly efficient sub-sample (coreset) for the $k$-means clustering problem in $d$ dimensional space. This innovative technique, which processes data points at a rate of $O(\log k + \log N)$ per input point, produces a coreset of approximately $k \cdot d$ dimensions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our coreset-based approach by developing a corresponding approximation algorithm that achieves a target standard for the $k$-means objective function while keeping the computational cost remarkably low at roughly $O(k \cdot d^2 \log k + k \cdot d^3 \log^2 N)$ for large datasets. Additionally, we establish the theoretical guarantee that our coreset construction yields a representation that is precise to a factor of $O(\frac{\log k}{\log N})^{\frac{1}{2}}$ with respect to the optimal solution, thereby further refining the previous bound obtained through a more complex, multi-pass approach.

In large-scale grid worlds, an agent can split the environment into smaller regions, effectively creating a hierarchical framework of states and sub-states. By doing so, the agent's decision-making process can be simplified by only considering the overall pattern of its movements and the target's movements, rather than individual actions. This approach can be particularly advantageous in pursuit-evasion scenarios, where the agent must navigate a vast space to catch the evader. By applying this technique, known as state partitioning, the agent can enhance its chances of success by reducing the number of actions it needs to take. However, implementing state partitioning correctly requires determining the optimal way to divide the grid, a problem that is challenging to solve directly. As an alternative solution, we propose using a simple and adaptive method called grid partitioning by state difference (GPSD), which enables the agent to dynamically adjust the way it splits the grid based on its observations of the environment and the target's behavior. This approach can be seen as a way to adapt the existing method of dynamic state partitioning to the specific scenario described above. Both theoretical and empirical studies have shown that GPSD enables the agent to effectively manage the grid partitioning, leading to better outcomes in pursuit-evasion games compared to the current standard method of dynamic state partitioning.

A theoretical framework that expands on the parton distribution function (PDF) approach has been developed to accurately describe the production of W and Z bosons in high-energy collisions. This model-based method enhances the standard PDF method by incorporating universal corrections, as evidenced by recent precise measurements from the LHC. To better align with experimental data, the non-perturbative quark distribution, represented by the tension parameter, has been allowed to vary. Utilizing relevant PDF sets and a fixed number of universal correction parameters, our study demonstrated the capability to replicate current precision data from the LHC with small statistical uncertainties. Furthermore, this study has been extended to predict the production of W and Z bosons in future collisions at the LHC and a 100 TeV proton collider.

When applying a single learned dynamics model across multiple tasks from the same domain, a potential drawback is that it may prioritize the skills of the task it was trained on, potentially hindering performance in other tasks. This phenomenon is known as dynamic model overfitting. To address this challenge, we introduce a new method called Adaptive Dynamics Model Adaptation (ADMA), which allows a single dynamics model to adapt to a new task without the need for additional training data. ADMA employs a specialized policy to update the parameters of the dynamics model based on the actions taken during exploration in the new environment. By combining the updates from the policy and the data-driven corrections, our method achieves a dynamic model that effectively adapts to the new task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ADMA in transferring a pre-trained dynamics model to a new task through experiments conducted in various 2D navigation scenarios and a 3D locomotion simulation.

which was introduced by Rosser, can be replicated using just his version of 
Godel's first incompleteness theorem. Consequently, we establish that attempts to 
strengthen the first incompleteness theorem beyond Rosser's extension are 
unsuccessful. Additionally, our proof provides a novel explanation for Rosser's 
extension of Godel's first incompleteness theorem that sophisticated readers may 
find informative.

This communication provides an extension of Hadamard's three circles theorem to real-valued functions in higher dimensions that belong to the class of Riemannian monogenic functions. Specifically, it will be shown that an application of the Cauchy-Pompeiu operator can be beneficial in proving a more general version of Hadamard's three circles theorem. The connection between the Cauchy-Pompeiu operator and the Dirac operator in higher dimensions will also be explored. The paper's final section outlines future research directions related to Hadamard's three circles theorem in higher dimensions.

Imaging the contents of a unknown box using passive sensor data from a target motion scenario is a significant challenge.  Typically, a statistical approach is employed to tackle this problem by modeling sensor-data probabilities and the imaged-object probabilities as two separate distributions.  However, the shortcoming of this method is that it yields an underdetermined problem with infinitely many possible solutions.  To address this difficulty, a novel technique based on a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN (RCWGAN) is proposed.  This technique generates artificial posterior samples by introducing a constraint on the conditional Wasserstein distance between the predicted posterior distribution and the sensor-data probability distribution.  To train this model, an additional constraint on the conditional Wasserstein distance between the data generated from the predicted posterior distribution and the actual sensor-data is imposed.  As evidenced by the simulation results, this method yields a determined solution and significantly improves the accuracy of imaging reconstructions.

This study investigates the concepts of invariance and robustness in fractional order systems, particularly focusing on the problem of maintaining system properties within specified linear subspaces. The team of researchers developing this work highlights the need for certain conditions to be met, such as the subspaces in question being commutative with the fractional operator, as well as requiring that the system's input and output be confined to these subspaces. A key finding revealed in the paper shows that when input signals are restricted to a particular subspace, the system's output will also remain within the same subspace. A notable contribution of this research includes developing new approaches to evaluate the robustness of fractional order systems, including systems with time-varying components. A recommendation is made for further exploration into extending these concepts to nonlinear settings.

Using high-resolution radio telescopes, researchers studied the surroundings of an ancient radio pulse, PSR B1133+16, made nearly 40 years ago. By observing this pulse, its team discovered numerous strong radio signals had interacted with the associated neutron star, revealing a rich and complex environment containing at least 150 individual scattering screens, a remarkable discovery given the vast distance of this environment from Earth. To better understand these findings, the team compared them to previous observations of the same pulse, combining the data and finding it matches the expectations of an expanding plasma cloud, known as the pulsar wind nebula, surrounding the star. Compared to earlier observations, this new data revealed a smaller level of radio signal weakening, suggesting the nebula is more extensive than initially thought, with researchers estimating it measures over 40 billion kilometers in diameter.

Deep neural networks have effectively modeled complex signals such as speech, but their effectiveness is largely attributed to their ability to detect periodic patterns present in speech. Conversely, a network structured to identify the fundamental frequency of speech may efficiently capture its underlying dynamics. This paper presents a novel, cascaded network with periodic analysis modules at its core, capable of deconstructing synthetic speech signals into their fundamental frequency components. This network's ability to recover the exact time frames and magnitude spectra from its compressed representations was examined and yielded notable improvements in a benchmark task.

We introduce a concept called'shadow' that extends the idea found in topological Hochschild homology, specifically to bicategorical settings. This leads to the development of a new theory called bicategorical topological Hochschild homology, which we can view as a part of the broader bicategorical framework known as the'spectrum of shadows'. This spectrum preserves key properties from its categorical counterpart, particularly exhibiting excisivity properties. By applying bicategorical topological Hochschild homology, we derive an enhanced understanding of the relationship between bicategorical toroidal functors and bicategorical functors of trace functors.

VGG-SS is a comprehensive dataset featuring 31,696 human-annotated sound clips from 1,926 distinct sources, including both natural and man-made objects. This benchmark surpasses existing datasets in size and scope, offering clear categorization based on source attributes. Developed specifically for the task of unconditional sound source separation, VGG-SS demonstrates superior performance compared to leading models trained on existing datasets. Our record-breaking dataset stands out due to several key features: compared to 13,000 clip FFDataset, VGG-SS boasts a substantially larger collection of training clips (by a factor of 2.4) and a more comprehensive set of source categories (by a factor of 7.5). Notably, VGG-SS excels over other datasets in the organization of source attributes, with a hierarchical structure consisting of 51 distinct categories. This structure's effectiveness is substantiated by improved performance when using it to guide the training of unconditional sound source separation models. The code and dataset are available for public use at: https://github.com/vgg/SS.

This research introduces the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), a novel model that operates within the Poincaré disk model of hyperbolic geometry. LGCN surpasses the existing hierarchy of hyperbolic graph convolutional networks by refining node feature representation and eliminating the requirement for explicit coordinate transformation in graph convolution operations. Specifically, LGCN enhances the precision of comparisons between the adjacency matrix and the Laplace-Beltrami operator by employing a non-parametric comparison based on the geometric interpretation of the adjacency matrix in the Poincaré disk model. This leads to a direct convolution operation that bypasses the need for re-projecting learned coordinates. As a result, LGCN exhibits superior performance compared to rival hyperbolic GCNs in terms of both accuracy and simplicity. Experimental evaluations on datasets obtained through graph generation and real-world scenarios demonstrate the advantages of LGCN.

We address several inverse problems linked to the determination of a boundary control or an unknown part of the boundary in a time-like domain. Our primary objective is to establish conditions for unique solution identification and provide a stability estimate. To accomplish this, we leverage a modified observability inequality, which we derive using the Carleman weight in a parabolic setting. This inequality enables us to establish log-regularity properties and, under specific assumptions, establish the uniqueness of the unknown boundary segment. To achieve these results, we must navigate certain limitations imposed by the absence of an observable uniqueness property in some cases.

The Tsallis distribution has widespread applicability across various social systems, yet the underlying reasons for its broad scope are not well understood. This study proposes a framework for interpreting the Tsallis distribution in general terms, then applies it to specific cases of social behavior, such as the Tsallis distribution's appearance in opinions and cultural expressions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this approach can be used to uncover underlying dynamics and parameters from observed data.

We introduce a linearized gravity theory that includes mass terms for gravitational perturbations. We then apply this model to a static and dense droplet, and map it to a $d$-dimensional sphere using conformal transformations. We subsequently analyze the inclusion of mass terms for a general $d$-dimensional sphere, and thereby derive the degrees of freedom for linearized gravity within the droplet. We also compare our results to previously established findings for the Riemann metric.

For classical systems with a finite number of Hamiltonian dynamics, multiple quantum equilibrium states can arise from a single classical configuration due to different sequences of discrete time steps. Research has categorized their quantum dynamics into four types: reversible, thermodynamically neutral, entangling, and dissipative. This distinction's significance is particularly evident when considering quantum systems in contact with quantum environments, as it affects the stability of quantum equilibrium states and associated quantum work values. A comprehensive understanding of these dynamics is crucial for extending classical thermodynamics to quantum systems.

A common analogy to explain negative temperature relies on a metaphor of two energy levels where a system with a higher population in a lower energy state is compared to a situation where people prefer hotter food. We contend that this analogy is misleading and offer an alternative based on two energy levels where the population is concentrated, indicating a divergence or singularity rather than a negative temperature. We propose using the analogy of a system with two energy levels, one where the population drops off sharply, representing a situation that could exhibit negative temperature behavior, in line with the mathematical definition. We suggest that physicists reevaluate the analogy they use to illustrate this concept to students.

We introduce a scenario where a minimal dark sector makes up a significant component of the universe's matter density. This scenario is set within a framework that incorporates both dark parity symmetry and dark matter-seesaw mechanisms. We demonstrate how the incorporation of a substantial dark sector affects the vacuum stability of the electroweak force and dark parity symmetry. Furthermore, we examine the constraints placed on this scenario by both the observed dark matter density and the demise of the vacuum state due to the incorporation of a scalar sector. Our analysis is carried out within a framework that utilizes an effective potential approach, with an incorporation of both loop corrections and the impact of both dark and standard model sectors on the vacuum stability.

To understand the dependence of spin-orbit coupling on the position within transition metal oxides, it's crucial to consider both the fundamental properties of the spin-orbit effect and interaction-driven renormalizations. In this work, we examine the spin-orbit coupling in a general sense, taking into account both its intrinsic features and the influence of electron correlations and crystal field splitting. We studied a hypothetical material, strontium ruthenates (Sr$_2$Ruthenate), in both its 5d-electron and 4d-electron configurations, using a combination of DMFT and lattice models. Our findings indicate that, while the spin-orbit coupling can seem errant in certain localized situations, it returns to its intrinsic value when strong interactions are present in a double-peaked density of states scenario. Notably, we discovered that the spin-orbit coupling can be influenced by the filling level of d-orbitals and the asymmetry of the density of states, which may impact the robustness of the time-reversal broken phase in strontium ruthenates.

We introduce a new concept called the "relative $I$-function" which can be applied to toric complete intersections featuring smooth divisors. Subsequent to this discovery, we demonstrate the applicability of the technique to a specific case study, involving toric complete intersections from non-degenerate, irreducible components with specific properties. Ultimately, we establish a meaningful relationship between the relative $I$-functions of these toric complete intersections. Moreover, we provide the detailed analysis of a particular example, which arises from a specific hyperplane intersection within a 3-dimensional space, filled with triangular prisms, and feature a specific divisor configuration. This example allows us to computationally derive the formula for its associated relative $I$-function.

Using generative models, particularly GANs, medics can manipulate authentic medical images by altering the latent code, which may affect the model's ability to accurately represent medical conditions from images. This study investigates the potential misinformation that can be introduced into medical diagnoses made using artificial neural networks, specifically by misclassifying a patient's condition when a healthy image is created from a genuine image. To tackle this challenge, methods such as restricting code modification or using robust models are proposed. Our main contribution introduces a novel GAN-based medical image manipulation technique that combines the effects of both methods. This study's results show that it is possible to devise a technique that effectively prevents the dissemination of incorrect medical information to the neural network even when the manipulation is extreme. Our research also explores the connection between the technique's efficacy and the way medical conditions are represented in the latent code space. Finally, we apply this technique to a real-world case study involving the manipulation of 3D stroke lesions.

The primary objective of the ViDaExpert system lies in facilitating the
interpretation of multidimensional data for various tasks such as identifying
key variables, visualizing complex relationships, and differentiating distinct
groups of objects. This system offers a user-friendly interface to achieve these
goals by utilizing a set of advanced techniques including self-organizing maps,
decision trees, and cluster analysis. Developed using Java, ViDaExpert provides
a convenient graphical user interface that enables users to load, manage, and
analyze their data effectively. The system's features can be utilized in various
fields including economics, finance, and biology for in-depth analysis of any
dataset.
